title: how make world safer ai 2026 09 07
author: Hugo Dixon
text:
TINOS, Greece, Sept 7 (Reuters Breakingviews) - Artificial intelligence may already be running out of control. Managing the risks requires an international regulatory regime. To get there, the United States will have to first accept the dangers and then cut a deal with China.
AI has huge advantages. But the latest models are capable of sophisticated cyberattacks and could also help produce new deadly pathogens if they get into the hands ​of militant or criminal groups. Autonomous AI agents may increasingly go on the rampage themselves, as some OpenAI ones did in July. Aggressive countries may also use them to enhance their military might.
The effort to ‌control AI is weak and patchy. The European Union has an AI act and several countries have safety institutes. But President Donald Trump does not want to regulate the industry, partly because its investments are powering the American economy. Goldman Sachs analysts estimate
, opens new tab
 the capital spending splurge will account for 2.8% of U.S. output in 2028, up from 1.8% this year. The United States is also worried that placing constraints on its leading AI labs could allow second-placed China to catch up.
Washington temporarily imposed export controls on Anthropic’s top Mythos and Fable models in June, citing national security. ​And last month it created a framework
, opens new tab
 where leading AI companies can give the government access to new models 30 days before wider release. But this is only voluntary. Last week the Trump administration pressed members of the G20 group ​of leading economies to take a hands-off approach to AI regulation.
Meanwhile, although Beijing regulates its AI industry, Chinese companies such as Qwen, Moonshot AI and DeepSeek are leading
, opens new tab
 producers of so-called “open-weight” ⁠AI models. Users can download them onto local computers and disable their safety features. This makes them harder to control.
Running wild
Breakneck competition between individual companies - and between the United States and China - is fuelling a race to create increasingly advanced models. ​The two top U.S. firms, Anthropic and OpenAI, are aiming for initial public offerings in coming months that could value each at $1 trillion or more.
In a particularly disturbing incident in July, a swarm of OpenAI’s agents escaped a supposedly secure “sandbox” and hacked Hugging Face, ​an open-source platform. Many tried to cover their tracks. Despite this, OpenAI last week launched its latest model, Astra, while cautioning that it sometimes attempts to evade human monitoring and is more likely to intentionally disguise its reasoning.
A group of industry insiders including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is so worried that in July it called on
, opens new tab
 Washington to support an international effort to slow down frontier AI development. Meanwhile, two former U.S. Treasury Secretaries, Henry Paulson and Robert Rubin, last week wrote
, opens new tab
 in the Washington Post that “self-regulation in competitive markets simply doesn’t work, because restraint is not what ​markets reward.”
The OpenAI/Hugging Face incident shows external regulators need to monitor the development and training of AI systems, not just the final products. A proper AI regulatory regime would therefore vet advanced models before they were launched and ban those that ​were not safe.
Independent authorities would even need the power to order the entire industry to pause development so that work on safety can catch up. To do this effectively, the watchdogs would have to be sufficiently well funded to hire AI experts who could otherwise ‌earn fortunes in ⁠the industry.
Mistrust but verify
Getting to such a regime requires a change in mindset in Washington. Trump would have to go against his deregulatory instincts and ignore lobbying by well-connected tech companies. The United States and China would also have to cooperate, which is hard because of their superpower rivalry and lack of mutual trust.
Paulson and Rubin argue mistrust could paradoxically be an advantage. They say mutual mistrust between the United States and Soviet Union spurred a pact to limit strategic nuclear weapons during the Cold War.
Sebastian Mallaby, author of “The Infinity Machine: Demis Hassabis, DeepMind and the Quest for Superintelligence”, a book about the AI pioneer, argues that Washington and Beijing have a common interest in stopping advanced models getting into the hands of bad actors. Neither wants ​criminal or militant groups to launch cyberattacks or develop pathogens.
Though ​Trump says he will discuss AI with Xi Jinping when ⁠the Chinese president comes to the United States on September 24, there are huge obstacles to a deal. One issue is how to stop cheating. While satellites can spot the vast data centres that train advanced models, it is harder to know what is happening inside them. That will require either inspections or some technical fix.
Another problem is that it may be necessary ​to freeze the development of open-weight models before they become too powerful. China might oppose that, since this is where it has an edge - though any pause would also ​hurt U.S. companies such as Meta ⁠and Nvidia.
Carrots and sticks
Washington could try carrots and sticks to get Beijing on board. For example, it could relax its existing export controls on advanced semiconductors if China agrees a verifiable deal but heap on the pressure if the People’s Republic refuses to play ball.
China’s weakest point is lack of adequate computing power. So Trump could tighten chip controls to reduce smuggling and deny Chinese companies access to U.S. data centres. He could also make it harder for Chinese companies to train their models on U.S. ones and even ⁠ban Americans from ​using Chinese ones.
Of course, Xi might retaliate. That is what he did last year when the United States imposed punitive tariffs, forcing Trump to retreat. For ​these reasons, the chances of an effective regulatory regime in the short run are slim.
This is not the first time that governments have regulated risky technologies. But it often takes a crisis to bring about change. States tightened pharmaceutical regulation after the thalidomide drug for morning sickness caused birth defects in the ​1950s and 1960s. Financial services oversight became more intrusive after the 2008 global financial crisis.
Even more is probably at stake with AI. All the more reason to take action before disaster hits.
